# Frequency polygons {#sec-freq-poly} :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false} ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** :::
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](frequency_polygons_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: :::: ## Description A frequency polygon is a plot that displays data distributions using points connected by straight lines. It's similar to a histogram but is more commonly used to compare data across multiple sets. A legend is often included to differentiate between various data sets. Frequency polygons are used to assess [symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) and [skewness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewness). ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} install.packages("palmerpenguins") library(palmerpenguins) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: ::: {.column-margin} ![Artwork by Allison Horst](www/lter_penguins.png){fig-align="right" width="65%"} ::: The `penguins` data. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} penguins <- palmerpenguins::penguins glimpse(penguins) #> Rows: 344 #> Columns: 8 #> $ species Adelie, Adelie, Adelie… #> $ island Torgersen, Torgersen, … #> $ bill_length_mm 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, … #> $ bill_depth_mm 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, … #> $ flipper_length_mm 181, 186, 195, NA, 193… #> $ body_mass_g 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, … #> $ sex male, female, female, … #> $ year 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007… ``` ::: ::: ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: 1. Create labels with `labs()` 2. Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` 3. Map `flipper_length_mm` to the `x` axis 4. Add the `geom_freqpoly()` layer ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} labs_freqpoly <- labs( title = "Adult foraging penguins", subtitle = "Distribution of flipper length", x = "Flipper length (millimeters)") ggp2_freqpoly <- ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm)) + geom_freqpoly() ggp2_freqpoly + labs_freqpoly ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](frequency_polygons_files/figure-html/create_graph_freq_poly-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: Experiment to see how many `bins` fit your variable’s distribution. ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ggp2_freqpoly_bins45 <- ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm)) + geom_freqpoly(bins = 45) ggp2_freqpoly_bins45 + labs_freqpoly ggp2_freqpoly_bins15 <- ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm)) + geom_freqpoly(bins = 15) ggp2_freqpoly_bins15 + labs_freqpoly ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](frequency_polygons_files/figure-html/bins_freq_poly-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](frequency_polygons_files/figure-html/bins_freq_poly-2.png){width=576} ::: :::
